items.title: Cities are typically 2-5 °C warmer than surrounding countryside
items.claim: What is the urban heat island effect?

options.text: A myth — cities are no warmer than rural areas

Cities are typically 2-5 °C warmer than surrounding rural areas (up to 10 °C at night in extremes) due to dark surfaces (low albedo), reduced evapotranspiration, anthropogenic heat and reduced sky view
Cities are colder than countryside due to shade
Only New York shows the effect

items.reveal:
Causes: low-albedo asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation; reduced vegetation cuts evaporative cooling; tall buildings trap re-emitted infrared (sky-view factor); waste heat from vehicles, buildings and air conditioning; thermal mass releases heat at night.

London during the August 2003 heatwave was around 4-9 °C warmer than surrounding countryside at night; UHI contributed to the death toll (around 2,000 excess deaths in the UK). Paris 2003 saw around 15,000 excess deaths.

Mitigation: green roofs, urban trees (Singapore, Melbourne), light-coloured surfaces (Los Angeles cool roofs), water features, ventilation corridors in city planning.
items.why: Urban climate is human-made microclimate. Climate change interacts with UHI to make heatwaves more dangerous in cities — a fast-rising public health hazard.

items.title: Coral reefs fix nitrogen and support a quarter of marine species
items.claim: What is the ecological importance of coral reefs?

options.text: They are aesthetic features with little ecological role

Reefs cover under 0.1% of the ocean floor but host around 25% of marine species; symbiotic cyanobacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen, fertilising nutrient-poor tropical waters; reefs also protect coasts from wave energy
Reefs are made entirely of dead material
Reefs occur only in polar oceans

items.reveal:
Reefs occupy around 284,000 km² globally — under 0.1% of the ocean — and yet host an estimated 4,000 fish species, 800 reef-building coral species, and uncounted invertebrates.

Cyanobacteria in coral tissues and on reef surfaces fix atmospheric nitrogen, providing essential nutrients in otherwise oligotrophic (nutrient-poor) tropical waters. The reefs function as 'oases' of productivity.

Mass bleaching events (1998, 2010, 2014-17, 2024) have hit major systems. The Great Barrier Reef has bleached in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Estimated coastal protection value is tens of billions of dollars annually.
items.why: Concentrated biodiversity means concentrated risk. Losing reefs means losing entire ecosystems — not just iconic species — and removing coastal protection from hundreds of millions of people.

items.title: Britain's climate is anomalously warm for its latitude
items.claim: London sits at 51 degrees North — the same latitude as Calgary, Canada (winters of -30 C). Why is London so much warmer?

options.text: The Gulf Stream and the wider North Atlantic Current transport tropical heat northward, with prevailing westerlies carrying it onshore
The North Sea acts as a giant heat reservoir from summer
Britain receives more solar radiation due to cloud cover patterns
The Jet Stream alone is responsible

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream originates in the Gulf of Mexico, feeds the North Atlantic Current, and as it cools and becomes saltier, sinks near Iceland and Greenland — driving the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). The energy transfer is roughly 1.3 petawatts, about 10,000 times UK electricity demand.

The AMOC has weakened measurably since the mid-20th century. A collapse would cool Britain dramatically while warming the tropics — a non-linear climate flip.
items.why: Climate is not just latitude. Ocean circulation is one of the largest energy-redistribution systems on the planet, and it's not guaranteed to keep running.
